title: Latent-Conditioned Parameterized Quantum Circuits as Universal Approximators for Distributions over Quantum States
authors: Quoc Hoan Tran, Koki Chinzei, Yasuhiro Endo, Hirotaka Oshima
abstract: Many applications in quantum simulation, quantum chemistry, and quantum machine learning require not a single quantum state but an ensemble of states characterizing the heterogeneity of a target system. Preparing such ensembles state-by-state is prohibitive in both variational and fault-tolerant settings, motivating a generative-modeling approach. We introduce latent-conditioned parameterized quantum circuits (LPQCs), a hybrid quantum-classical framework in which classical neural networks map a latent variable sampled from a prior distribution to the parameters of a parameterized quantum circuit. We prove that LPQCs are universal approximators for probability measures over density operators in the $1$-Wasserstein distance, extending classical universal approximation theorems to the quantum-distribution setting. We additionally introduce a multimodal latent prior and a mixture-of-experts circuit architecture, and show that it empirically alleviates the barren plateau problem during optimization. Numerical experiments validate the framework on a synthetic multi-cluster ensemble of mixed quantum states and on a QM9-derived ensemble of 3-D molecular structures. In these tasks, LPQC outperforms recent quantum generative baselines while remaining competitive with typical classical baselines at substantially reduced output dimensionality. By leveraging classical expressivity in the latent space, LPQCs offer a tractable route to quantum generative modeling.

infographic.key_insight: Latent-conditioned parameterized quantum circuits (LPQCs) use a classical latent variable to generate quantum circuit parameters, and are proven to universally approximate distributions over quantum states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical quantum generative modeling route for heterogeneous state ensembles in quantum simulation, chemistry, and machine learning without preparing each state individually.
method: Sample a latent variable from a prior distribution.
Use classical neural networks to map the latent code to quantum circuit parameters.
Generate quantum states with a parameterized quantum circuit; a multimodal prior and mixture-of-experts design help optimization and reduce barren plateaus.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation on a synthetic multi-cluster ensemble of mixed quantum states and a QM9-derived ensemble of 3-D molecular structures, with LPQC outperforming recent quantum baselines and remaining competitive with classical baselines at lower output dimensionality.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on effective latent prior design and circuit training, so optimization stability and scalability may still be challenging on larger, noisier quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Latent-Conditioned Parameterized Quantum Circuits as Universal Approximators for Distributions over Quantum States

title: Quantum optimization beyond QUBO for industrial logistics and scheduling
authors: Juan F. R. Hernandez, Pavle Nikacevic, Enrique Solano, Chinonso Onah, Agneev Guin, Arne-Christian Voigt
abstract: The increasing complexity of industrial scheduling and transport routing problems motivates the study of alternative optimization formulations and computational paradigms. In this work, we study how higher-order unconstrained binary optimization (HUBO) formulations of such problems map onto quantum optimization workflows in both noisy and fault-tolerant regimes. We consider three representative logistics and manufacturing use cases and formulate each as a HUBO problem. This captures process intricacies, such as highly correlated assembly-line scheduling rules, which are difficult to express faithfully with the standard quadratic (QUBO) form, while at the same time reducing the number of binary variables required in the quantum mapping, thus lowering qubit demand. We compare the HUBO formulations with corresponding QUBO encodings, highlighting a key trade-off: while HUBO reduces qubit requirements through compact binary encoding, it introduces higher-order interaction terms that increase circuit depth, limiting feasibility on current quantum hardware. The proposed formulations are validated using classical solvers across several problem instances and benchmark small routing problem instances using bias-field digitized counterdiabatic quantum optimization in classical simulation. We complement these results with a resource and scalability analysis, focusing on the capacitated vehicle routing problem as a representative large-scale industrial use case. Our analysis indicates that while HUBO formulations offer advantages in qubit scaling compared to QUBO encodings, their practical implementation is constrained by gate fidelity, coherence, and circuit depth, making hybrid quantum-classical workflows and early fault-tolerant quantum hardware the most plausible settings for their practical use.

infographic.key_insight: Higher-order binary optimization (HUBO) can encode industrial logistics and scheduling more compactly than QUBO, reducing qubit demand but increasing circuit complexity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For real-world routing and scheduling, HUBO may preserve constraints more faithfully and improve resource scaling, especially in hybrid quantum-classical workflows.
method: Formulated three representative logistics/manufacturing problems as HUBO models.
Compared HUBO encodings against corresponding QUBO formulations on qubit count and interaction order.
Benchmarked small routing instances with bias-field digitized counterdiabatic quantum optimization in simulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper validates the formulations with classical solvers across multiple problem instances and performs a resource/scalability analysis using capacitated vehicle routing as a representative large-scale case.
infographic.watch_item: HUBO’s higher-order terms raise circuit depth, so current noisy hardware may not support practical execution without improved fidelity or early fault-tolerant devices.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum optimization beyond QUBO for industrial logistics and scheduling

title: Variational Quantum Models for Knowledge Graph Embeddings on NISQ Devices
authors: Guido Bellomo, Martín Santesteban, Patricio Bruno, Santiago Cifuentes, Gustavo Martín Bosyk
abstract: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) combine quantum circuits with classical optimization to tackle problems that may benefit from the capabilities of near-term quantum hardware. In knowledge graph embedding, recent proposals based on this approach follow a similar overall architecture but differ in the way they compute the score function and in the number of qubits they require. One design uses $n+1$ qubits and obtains the score through a switch test on an ancillary qubit, while another employs $2n+1$ qubits and applies a swap test between two registers. In both cases, entities and relations are represented in a Hilbert space of dimension $d = 2^n$, with comparable computational cost and the same mean squared error loss. This work introduces a unified framework that captures the two schemes and makes it possible to explore new variants. Within this setting, we propose an alternative that keeps the intuitive meaning of the score function while dispensing with ancillary qubits and entangled measurements. The result is a model better suited to current NISQ devices, reducing hardware demands without sacrificing interpretability.

infographic.key_insight: A unified variational quantum framework shows that knowledge-graph embedding scores can be computed with fewer qubits and simpler measurements while preserving the intended score interpretation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The proposed design lowers hardware requirements for NISQ-era quantum devices, making quantum knowledge-graph embeddings more practical to implement and test on near-term systems.
method: Unifies prior KGE variational quantum models into a single architecture.
Compares switch-test and swap-test score estimation with different qubit budgets.
Introduces an alternative score computation that avoids ancillary qubits and entangled measurements.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparable computational cost and the same mean squared error loss across the baseline schemes, motivating the unified comparison.
infographic.watch_item: The reduced-qubit design may simplify hardware execution, but its practical advantage still depends on circuit fidelity and optimization stability on real NISQ devices.
infographic.paper_title: Variational Quantum Models for Knowledge Graph Embeddings on NISQ Devices

title: EFaaS: A Quantum-Classical Serverless Entangled Scheduler for Hybrid Variational Algorithms
authors: Abolfazl Younesi, Nouhaila Innan, Alberto Marchisio, Muhammad Shafique
abstract: As quantum computing enters the Utility Era, realizing near-term advantage relies heavily on Hybrid Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs). These algorithms require a tightly coupled, iterative loop between a classical CPU optimizer and a Quantum Processing Unit (QPU). However, current quantum cloud access models are bottlenecked by decoupled batch-queues that sever this loop, introducing massive Time-to-Next-Shot (TTNS) latency. This delay inflates convergence time from minutes to hours and exposes the computation to quantum hardware drift, degrading algorithmic fidelity. Unlike prior works that rely on resource-wasting static hardware reservations or state-oblivious stateless functions, we propose EFaaS, a novel serverless middleware designed specifically for hybrid quantum workflows. EFaaS fundamentally departs from existing architectures by treating classical parameter optimization and quantum circuit execution as entangled, session-aware events. Our main technical innovations are threefold: (1) a Calibration-Aware placement strategy that dynamically routes circuits to QPUs with warm calibration caches, circumventing cold-start penalties, (2) a Dual-Resource Fair Queuing scheduler that maximizes quantum utilization by strictly prioritizing active iterative loops, and (3) the "EF-QuantumFuture" programming abstraction, a novel primitive enabling classical speculative execution to mask compute latency. Across the evaluated baselines, EFaaS achieves TTNS reductions of 11.4%-94.3%, QDC gains of 2.02%-15.78% points, and convergence speedups of 83.2%-98.3%, while eliminating drift penalties.

infographic.key_insight: EFaaS turns hybrid quantum-classical VQA execution into a session-aware serverless workflow to slash latency between classical optimization steps and QPU shots.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It is relevant for building practical quantum cloud systems that reduce time-to-next-shot, improve hardware utilization, and stabilize near-term algorithm convergence.
method: Calibration-aware placement routes jobs to QPUs with warm calibration caches.
Dual-resource fair queuing prioritizes active iterative quantum-classical loops.
EF-QuantumFuture enables speculative classical execution to hide latency.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports TTNS reductions of 11.4%-94.3%, QDC gains of 2.02%-15.78 percentage points, and convergence speedups of 83.2%-98.3% across baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The approach likely depends on accurate session tracking, calibration-state visibility, and scheduler integration across heterogeneous quantum cloud backends.
infographic.paper_title: EFaaS: A Quantum-Classical Serverless Entangled Scheduler for Hybrid Variational Algorithms

title: Thermodynamic-limit dispersion relations on trapped-ion quantum hardware
authors: Lucas Marti, Sumeet, Stefan Wolf, K. P. Schmidt, Michael J. Hartmann
abstract: We run a numerical linked-cluster expansion with a quantum algorithm (NLCE+QA), computing ground-state energies and one quasi-particle dispersions in the thermodynamic limit using a 20-qubit trapped-ion quantum processing unit (QPU). The NLCE+QA framework extracts thermodynamic-limit properties from small-cluster calculations, making it naturally suited for near-term quantum devices. Projector-based block-diagonalization schemes such as projective cluster-additive transformation (PCAT) are essential to NLCE+QA, and they involve matrix inversion and square root operations that amplify measurement noise. A central question is therefore whether current hardware can provide expectation values that are accurate enough to withstand non-linear classical post-processing. We explore this challenge for the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) in one dimension, on a ladder geometry, as well as in a longitudinal field in one dimension. For the quantum algorithm, we consider adiabatic state preparation (ASP), as well as a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) trained on a classical device. The final expectation values are obtained from the QPU, using a novel alternative to the Hadamard test that we name the CX-test. We explore the regimes currently attainable on quantum devices and comment on the improvements needed for quantum computers to achieve results beyond classical reach.

infographic.key_insight: A 20-qubit trapped-ion QPU can supply expectation values for NLCE+QA that reconstruct thermodynamic-limit ground-state energies and a quasi-particle dispersion, but only if classical post-processing remains numerically stable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This shows how near-term quantum hardware could be used as a subroutine for scalable materials and condensed-matter calculations that extrapolate from small clusters to infinite systems.
method: NLCE+QA to extract thermodynamic-limit observables from small-cluster computations
PCAT-style projector-based block diagonalization for energies and dispersion relations
CX-test readout on the QPU, with ASP and VQE as state-preparation approaches
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical results for TFIM and related 1D/ladder settings, comparing QPU-derived expectation values under adiabatic state preparation and classical-trained VQE to assess whether they survive noise-sensitive nonlinear post-processing.
infographic.watch_item: Matrix inversion and square-root steps in PCAT can amplify measurement noise, so hardware readout precision is a key bottleneck before the approach can outperform classical methods.
infographic.paper_title: Thermodynamic-limit dispersion relations on trapped-ion quantum hardware

title: Programmable Dissipation via Partial Quantum Error Correction
authors: Sameer Dambal, Michael AD Taylor, Yu Zhang
abstract: Noise is typically treated as the adversary of quantum information processing. For open quantum dynamics, however, dissipation is part of the target physics, creating a tension with fault-tolerant architectures designed to suppress decoherence. Here we show that logical noise can instead be turned into a calibrated resource. We treat the error-correction cycle as a programmable primitive: one fault-tolerant round induces a logical completely positive trace-preserving map, and decoder/recovery randomization generates a controllable family of logical channels whose convex mixtures realize Kraus-channel mixing. This enables direct compilation of target dissipators into effective logical dynamics without explicit ancilla qubits for encoding the bath degree of freedoms. We derive an accuracy criterion for multi-step simulation in which the code distance is chosen so that uncontrolled logical errors remain a small fraction of the intended dissipation per step, rather than being driven below an arbitrarily small closed-system tolerance. Partial quantum error correction thus repurposes fault-tolerant structure to sculpt dissipation, offering a resource-efficient route to quantum simulation of open quantum systems.

infographic.key_insight: Partial quantum error correction can turn fault-tolerant error-correction cycles into a programmable source of controlled logical dissipation instead of only suppressing noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a resource-efficient way to compile target open-system dynamics directly at the logical level without introducing explicit bath ancilla qubits.
method: Run one fault-tolerant error-correction round to induce a logical CPTP map.
Randomize decoder/recovery choices to generate a controllable family of logical channels.
Mix these channels convexly to realize target Kraus-channel dissipators and set code distance so residual logical errors stay below the intended dissipation per step.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical derivation of an accuracy criterion for multi-step simulation and a compilation framework for target dissipators, rather than a numerical benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance still depends on choosing a code distance that keeps unintended logical errors small relative to the desired dissipation, which may be challenging on noisy hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Programmable Dissipation via Partial Quantum Error Correction

title: Overcoming the Matrix-Product-State Encoding Barrier via DMRG-Guided Probabilistic Imaginary-Time Evolution
authors: Masari Watanabe, Hirofumi Nishi, Taichi Kosugi, Shinji Tsuneyuki, Yu-ichiro Matsushita
abstract: Ground-state preparation is a fundamental task in quantum simulation, because the overlap of the prepared state with the true ground state significantly affects the overall cost of subsequent quantum algorithms. We propose a three-stage framework in which a matrix product state (MPS) of an $N$-site system obtained by the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) is loaded onto an $N$-qubit quantum register through an optimization-free matrix product disentangler (MPD) encoding circuit, and the residual error is then reduced by probabilistic imaginary-time evolution (PITE). We demonstrate that the central-bond Schmidt rank of intermediate states during MPS encoding grows logistically with the number of layers. Its inflection point $L^{*}$ marks the boundary of the efficient encoding regime. Beyond this point, the gain in fidelity slows rapidly, and the number of additional MPD layers required to reach a target infidelity $\varepsilon$ empirically scales as $\mathcal{O}(N^5\log(N/\varepsilon))$. To avoid this encoding-only tail, we stop the encoder at $L^{*}$ and suppress the remaining excited-state components by PITE, with the linear PITE schedule fixed deterministically from the ground-state energy, the effective gap, and the reference overlap estimated by DMRG. Numerical experiments on the spin-$1/2$ staggered-field Heisenberg chain show that the framework avoids very deep encoding circuits and substantially suppresses the post-selection overhead intrinsic to PITE. Combining classical preprocessing by DMRG, optimization-free MPS encoding, and deterministically scheduled PITE, the present framework offers a practical hybrid route to ground-state preparation in quantum simulation.

infographic.key_insight: DMRG finds a strong MPS starting point, and stopping MPS encoding at the logistic inflection point before using PITE avoids the deepest and least efficient part of state preparation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This hybrid workflow reduces circuit depth and post-selection cost, making ground-state initialization more practical for near-term quantum simulation pipelines.
method: Use DMRG to compute an N-site ground-state MPS and estimate overlap/gap parameters.
Encode the MPS onto qubits with an optimization-free matrix-product disentangler (MPD) circuit up to the inflection layer L*.
Apply deterministically scheduled probabilistic imaginary-time evolution (PITE) to remove remaining excited-state error.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests on the spin-1/2 staggered-field Heisenberg chain show that the approach avoids very deep encoding circuits and significantly lowers the post-selection overhead of PITE.
infographic.watch_item: The method depends on accurate classical preprocessing from DMRG and on problem-specific estimates of the gap and overlap, so performance may degrade when those quantities are hard to obtain or the target state is not well approximated by a low-bond-dimension MPS.
infographic.paper_title: Overcoming the Matrix-Product-State Encoding Barrier via DMRG-Guided Probabilistic Imaginary-Time Evolution

title: Digital Quantum Simulation of the quantum $β$-FPUT Lattice: Formulation and Resource Estimation
authors: Kiratholly Nandakumar Madhav Sharma, Juan Manuel Aguiar Hualde, Julian van Velzen, Phalgun Lolur
abstract: Heat conduction in low-dimensional systems exhibits strong deviations from Fourier behavior due to anharmonicity and long-lived vibrational correlations, challenging conventional computational approaches. The $β$-Fermi--Pasta--Ulam--Tsingou ($β$-FPUT) chain provides a minimal nonlinear lattice model for studying anomalous transport, yet its quantum real-time dynamics remain difficult to access with classical methods. We develop a first-quantized digital quantum-simulation framework for the quantum $β$-FPUT lattice, targeting fault-tolerant quantum computers. By working directly with discretized lattice displacements rather than truncated phonon occupation spaces, the approach captures anharmonic interactions while avoiding bosonic encoding overheads. We construct Trotterized circuit blocks for real-time evolution and introduce a Hermitian quadrature decomposition of Fourier-mode displacement operators that enables shallow quantum circuits for mode-resolved displacement correlators. We analyze the quantum resources required for the full simulation and measurement workflow, providing qubit counts, gate complexity, circuit-depth and resource estimates as functions of system size and resolution within a fault-tolerant workflow. These results establish a concrete algorithmic blueprint for simulating quantum transport dynamics in nonlinear low-dimensional lattice models on fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: The paper presents a first-quantized, fault-tolerant quantum algorithm to simulate the real-time dynamics of the anharmonic b2-FPUT lattice directly in displacement space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a concrete resource-estimation blueprint for quantum transport simulation in nonlinear low-dimensional materials, helping map the hardware cost of future fault-tolerant implementations.
method: Use discretized lattice displacements instead of truncated phonon occupation encodings.
Construct Trotterized circuit blocks for time evolution of the b2-FPUT chain.
Apply a Hermitian quadrature decomposition to measure Fourier-mode displacement correlators with shallow circuits.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports qubit, gate-complexity, circuit-depth, and overall resource estimates as functions of system size and resolution, but does not present numerical benchmark results.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is framed for fault-tolerant quantum hardware, so its practicality depends on hardware scale, error correction overhead, and the cost of deep Trotter circuits.
infographic.paper_title: Digital Quantum Simulation of the quantum $β$-FPUT Lattice: Formulation and Resource Estimation

title: Quantum Networks Using Color Defects in Diamond: Principles, Progress, and Perspectives
authors: Ayan Majumder, Cem Güney Torun, Tim Schröder, Gregor Pieplow, Prem Kumar, Kasturi Saha
abstract: Large-scale quantum networks will enable entirely new applications of quantum information science in fields such as quantum communication, distributed quantum computing, sensing, and metrology. To build nodes of such networks, diamond color defects are one of the promising candidates. Their excellent optical properties, fast spin-qubit control, and long spin coherence times make them well-suited for quantum information processing and quantum memory applications. Additionally, recent advances in the heterogeneous integration of diamond nanophotonic structures with photonic integrated circuits have made these systems more efficient and well-suited for scalable quantum processor architectures. In this comprehensive review, we discuss the optical and spin properties of these systems, recent progress in the building blocks of quantum networks, and demonstrations of metropolitan-scale quantum networks, as well as the challenges associated with these systems at both the fundamental and experimental levels, along with potential solutions.

infographic.key_insight: Diamond color defects are promising quantum-network nodes because they combine strong optical interfaces, fast spin control, and long coherence times.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The review highlights a path toward scalable quantum hardware by integrating diamond nanophotonics with photonic integrated circuits for distributed quantum communication and processing.
method: Survey optical and spin properties of diamond color defects for network-node design.
Review recent progress in quantum-network building blocks and metropolitan-scale demonstrations.
Discuss integration strategies and remaining experimental/fundamental challenges.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract synthesizes prior demonstrations and system advances rather than reporting new experimental data or a single benchmark evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability still depends on overcoming material, fabrication, and heterogeneous-integration challenges at both the device and system levels.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Networks Using Color Defects in Diamond: Principles, Progress, and Perspectives

title: Non-Abelian Mixer for QAOA on Hybrid Oscillator-Qubit Quantum Processors
authors: Thinh Le, Hansika Weerasena, Jianqing Liu
abstract: The realization of universal control in hybrid oscillator-qubit quantum processors enables the systematic design and implementation of quantum algorithms. However, the algorithmic development for such platforms remains at an early stage. While the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) has been extensively studied in both continuous-variable (CV) and discrete-variable (DV) quantum systems, its development in the hybrid CV-DV setting remains limited. In this paper, we propose a hardware-native non-Abelian mixer for QAOA on hybrid CV-DV quantum processors and develop a corresponding hybrid ansatz for the Max-Cut problem. We evaluate the proposed ansatz on unweighted Erdős-Rényi graphs and benchmark it against the standard transverse-field mixer using the approximation ratio and optimal-solution probability. Across all graph sizes and Fock cutoffs in our simulations, the proposed non-Abelian mixer consistently improves both expected solution quality and the probability of sampling an optimal solution relative to the transverse-field mixer. These results indicate that the proposed non-Abelian mixer is a promising building block for QAOA on hybrid oscillator-qubit platforms.

infographic.key_insight: A hardware-native non-Abelian mixer for hybrid oscillator-qubit QAOA improves Max-Cut performance over the standard transverse-field mixer in simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work points to a practical control primitive for designing more effective QAOA circuits on emerging hybrid CV-DV quantum processors.
method: Propose a non-Abelian mixer tailored to hybrid oscillator-qubit hardware.
Build a hybrid QAOA ansatz for the Max-Cut problem.
Benchmark against the transverse-field mixer using approximation ratio and optimal-solution probability.
infographic.evidence_signal: In simulations on unweighted Erdős-Rényi graphs, across all tested graph sizes and Fock cutoffs, the proposed mixer consistently outperformed the transverse-field baseline on both expected solution quality and probability of sampling an optimal solution.
infographic.watch_item: Results are simulation-based and depend on Fock cutoff choices, so hardware noise and finite-level truncation effects still need experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Non-Abelian Mixer for QAOA on Hybrid Oscillator-Qubit Quantum Processors

title: Qubit-efficient variational algorithm for nuclear structure
authors: Chandan Sarma, Paul Stevenson
abstract: In this work, we compare three qubit-mapping strategies to study the structure of the nuclear ground state within the shell model description employing the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) approach. Although the initial point for different mappings is a Hamiltonian matrix in many-body particle basis or Slater determinant (SD) basis, the structure of the trial wavefunction and resource counts are different for each mapping. These three mappings are tested for a mid $p$-shell nucleus $^{10}$B and compared the quantum resources required to find the ground state for each mapping. Further, we extend the qubit-efficient mapping to study the ground state of one more mid $p$-shell nucleus $^{12}$C. We run circuits up to 26-qubits representing their ground states on a noisy simulator (IBM's FakeFez backend) and quantum hardware ($ibm\_fez$). The best post-error mitigated results from the hardware for $^{10}$B ground state is obtained following SD to qubit mapping with a percent error of 0.21 \%. The percent errors for the same state following cSD and pnSD mapping are 3.37 and 8.88 \%, respectively. On the other hand, following the cSD mapping, the post-error mitigated ground state energy of $^{12}$C is 6.82 \% away from the exact result. We further evaluate the fidelity of the VQE wavefunctions obtained from hardware with respect to the shell model wavefunctions for the cSD mapping. This cSD mapping can be useful for scaling the VQE algorithm for complex nuclei across different mass regions in terms of qubit efficiency.

infographic.key_insight: A qubit-efficient mapping for VQE can reproduce nuclear ground states with far fewer qubits, and the cSD mapping offers the best balance of resource efficiency and accuracy for mid p-shell nuclei.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study shows how choice of qubit mapping directly affects circuit depth, qubit count, and error sensitivity, making it highly relevant for scalable quantum simulation of nuclear structure on near-term hardware.
method: Compare three qubit mappings: SD, cSD, and pnSD for shell-model nuclear Hamiltonians.
Run VQE circuits up to 26 qubits on a noisy simulator and IBM quantum hardware.
Evaluate ground-state energies and wavefunction fidelity for 10B and 12C.
infographic.evidence_signal: Hardware post-error-mitigated results gave 0.21% error for 10B with SD mapping, versus 3.37% for cSD and 8.88% for pnSD; for 12C, cSD was 6.82% from exact.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends strongly on the chosen mapping and error mitigation, so scalability to larger nuclei may still be limited by hardware noise and circuit resource growth.
infographic.paper_title: Qubit-efficient variational algorithm for nuclear structure

title: Do We Really Need Quantum Machine Learning?: A Multidimensional Empirical Study
authors: Sudip Vhaduri, Ryan Gammon, Sayanton Dibbo
abstract: The rapid growth of computer vision and increasingly complex image recognition tasks has exposed fundamental computational limitations of classical machine learning models, motivating the exploration of quantum computing as an emerging new paradigm. This paper presents a comprehensive benchmarking study of classical and quantum machine learning models for image recognition on the MNIST handwritten digit dataset, evaluating both traditional models, a Classical Support Vector Machine (CSVM) and a Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM), and deep neural network models, a Classical Convolutional Neural Network (CCNN) and a Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN), across four performance dimensions: classification accuracy, computational runtime, parameter count, and memory requirements. Experiments are conducted as functions of both feature dimensionality and sample size, and across CPU and GPU execution environments, providing a controlled, multidimensional comparison to address gaps in prior work. For the SVM-based models, QSVM consistently outperforms CSVM in accuracy, reaching $\sim$ 0.90 versus $\sim$ 0.85 at 1,000 samples, with a higher computational cost. A feature count of 10 qubits and a sample size in the range of 200 -- 500 emerge as practical operating points that balance accuracy and runtime. For the neural network models, CCNN and QCNN achieve comparable classification accuracy, both exceeding 0.96 at 64 features and 60,000 samples, yet QCNN offers substantially superior parameter and memory efficiency, requiring $\sim$ 94\% fewer parameters and $\sim$ 75\% less memory than CCNN at higher feature counts, while incurring higher runtime. Across both model families, quantum models consistently outperform classical models by greater margins in accuracy as feature dimensionality or sample size increases.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum models showed a clear accuracy advantage over classical baselines on MNIST, but they traded that gain for higher runtime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For practical deployment, the study suggests quantum methods are most attractive when accuracy gains or resource efficiency justify added computational cost and quantum hardware complexity.
method: Benchmarked CSVM vs QSVM and CCNN vs QCNN on MNIST
Varied feature dimensionality, sample size, and execution environment (CPU/GPU)
Compared accuracy, runtime, parameter count, and memory requirements
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the evaluated settings, QSVM reached about 0.90 accuracy versus about 0.85 for CSVM at 1,000 samples, while QCNN and CCNN both exceeded 0.96 accuracy at 64 features and 60,000 samples.
infographic.watch_item: The reported quantum advantages come with higher runtime and depend on feature/sample scaling, so results may not transfer directly to larger real-world or hardware-constrained workloads.
infographic.paper_title: Do We Really Need Quantum Machine Learning?: A Multidimensional Empirical Study

title: Verifying Adversarial Robustness in Quantum Machine Learning: from theory to physical validation via a software tool
authors: Ji Guan, Mingsheng Ying
abstract: As with classical neural networks, quantum machine learning (QML) models are vulnerable to small input perturbations that can significantly alter output predictions. Certifying the robustness of QML models, particularly on NISQ hardware, is therefore a fundamental step toward trustworthy quantum AI. This chapter reviews our recently developed comprehensive formal framework for verifying adversarial robustness in QML. The core of this framework is a fidelity-based robustness lower bound computable directly from the measurement outcome distribution, which enables both formal verification and empirical estimation on real quantum devices. Additionally, the optimal bound can be computed via semidefinite programming (SDP) with full knowledge of the quantum machine learning models. We incorporate these results into: (1) an efficient formal verification framework; (2) VeriQR, the first dedicated QML robustness verification tool; and (3) the first experimental benchmark of quantum adversarial robustness on a 20-qubit superconducting processor. Together, these systematic advances enable scalable, physically grounded robustness evaluation of QML models.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a fidelity-based certification framework that can verify adversarial robustness of quantum machine learning models from measurement data and, when the full model is known, compute an optimal robustness bound via semidefinite programming.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical path to trustworthy QML on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware by enabling both theoretical guarantees and real-device robustness evaluation.
method: Derive a robustness lower bound from output measurement distributions.
Formulate the optimal bound as a semidefinite program with full model knowledge.
Package the framework into VeriQR for automated QML robustness verification and benchmarking.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports empirical validation through the first quantum adversarial robustness benchmark on a 20-qubit superconducting processor.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest certification requires full knowledge of the QML model, and real-device measurements may still be affected by noise and hardware imperfections.
infographic.paper_title: Verifying Adversarial Robustness in Quantum Machine Learning: from theory to physical validation via a software tool

title: Ground-state estimation of the Heisenberg model on frustrated lattices with Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization
authors: Calvin Brooks, Henry Zou, Trevor David Rhone
abstract: Quantum spin simulations of frustrated lattices remain challenging for both classical and quantum algorithms, particularly in parameter regimes relevant to quantum spin liquid (QSL) phases. In this work, we apply Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization (SKQD) to estimate the ground state of the antiferromagnetic XXZ Heisenberg model on the $J_1$--$J_2$ square lattice, the Kagome lattice, and a 1D chain, studying system sizes from 12 to 72 spins. In our application of SKQD, we identify a ZZ deformation of $Δ=2$ as a sufficiently sparse Hamiltonian and introduce two modifications to the SKQD framework tailored to spin models: a canonical bitstring compression scheme that preserves the effectiveness of configuration recovery under spin-flip degeneracy, and the use of multiple Krylov subspaces to improve ground state coverage without any increase in quantum resources. For the 1D chain and Kagome lattice, SKQD achieves sub-percent ground-state energy errors at system sizes up to 24 spins, including a relative error of $0.002\%$ on the 12-site Kagome lattice, surpassing the best prior VQE result of $0.01\%$ on the same system while requiring no variational optimization. SKQD further extends to system sizes well beyond the reach of prior quantum algorithm studies, reaching 72 spins across all three geometries. Beyond 24 spins, accuracy degrades to relative errors of $19\%$--$36\%$ at 72 sites, but the gradual scaling of error with system size suggests these limits are set by available shot budgets and circuit depth rather than fundamental algorithmic constraints. Although classical tensor network methods remain state-of-the-art for these models, this work establishes a new benchmark for quantum simulation of the frustrated Heisenberg model and demonstrates SKQD as a scalable, hardware-compatible approach for studying strongly correlated spin systems.

infographic.key_insight: Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization (SKQD) can estimate ground states of frustrated Heisenberg spin systems without variational optimization, achieving very high accuracy on small lattices and scaling to much larger ones than prior quantum studies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work shows a hardware-compatible path for near-term quantum simulation of strongly correlated spin models, with algorithmic tweaks that improve robustness under spin degeneracy and limited shot budgets.
method: Applied SKQD to the antiferromagnetic XXZ Heisenberg model on J1–J2 square, Kagome, and 1D chain lattices.
Used a ZZ deformation (Δ=2) to make the Hamiltonian sufficiently sparse for SKQD.
Added canonical bitstring compression and multiple Krylov subspaces to better recover configurations and improve ground-state coverage.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports sub-percent ground-state energy errors up to 24 spins, including 0.002% on the 12-site Kagome lattice, and extension to 72 spins with errors rising to about 19%–36% at the largest sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy degrades at larger system sizes, so results appear limited by shot budgets and circuit depth rather than the algorithm alone.
infographic.paper_title: Ground-state estimation of the Heisenberg model on frustrated lattices with Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization

title: On the question of noise as a resource in quantum computing
authors: J. Montes, F. Borondo, Gabriel G. Carlo
abstract: Noise is usually regarded as the main obstacle to achieving a scalable quantum advantage, but recent evidence in quantum reservoir computing [L. Domingo, F. Borondo, and G. G. Carlo. Taking advantage of noise in quantum reservoir computing, Scientific Reports, 13:8790, 2023] suggests that certain channels can, in appropriate regimes, improve performance by enriching the reservoir's effective dynamics. Motivated by this idea we propose a geometric mechanism to explain how non-unital noise applied together with a universal gate set leads to a faster approach to Haar-like distributions of the final states. We find that noise of this kind induces an effective volume expansion on the manifold of pure states. In order to intuitively understand this we use a minimal 1 qubit model where we take the amplitude damping channel and combine it with a renormalization rule that associates to each resulting mixed state a representative pure state. This composition defines a globally expanding nonlinear map on the space of pure states. We analytically derive the local area expansion factor and identify the global expansion threshold. Finally, we combine amplitude damping with the G3 = {H, T, CNOT} universal gate set to show how the approach to Haar-like behavior is faster in an appropriate parameter region. This leads us to propose noise as a possible resource in future quantum algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: Certain non-unital noise, when combined with universal gates, can accelerate the emergence of Haar-like output states by acting like an effective expansion on the pure-state manifold.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests noise may be harnessed as a controllable resource in quantum algorithms and reservoir-style processors, potentially improving state mixing and performance in some regimes.
method: Built a minimal 1-qubit model using amplitude damping plus a renormalization rule that maps mixed states back to representative pure states.
Analyzed the induced nonlinear map on pure states and derived the local area expansion factor and global expansion threshold.
Tested the idea with the universal gate set G3 = {H, T, CNOT} to study mixing toward Haar-like behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an analytical derivation of expansion conditions and shows that, in an appropriate parameter region, amplitude damping plus G3 leads to faster convergence toward Haar-like distributions.
infographic.watch_item: The effect relies on a specific non-unital noise channel and a renormalization scheme, so the advantage may be regime-dependent and not directly transferable to all hardware noise models.
infographic.paper_title: On the question of noise as a resource in quantum computing

title: A Variational Quantum Algorithm for Nonlinear Finite Element Analysis of Hyperelastic Materials
authors: Uditnarayan Kouskiya, Caglar Oskay
abstract: This manuscript explores a variational quantum formulation for nonlinear elasticity problems arising from hyperelastic material models, targeting near term noisy intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) devices. The approach leverages the potential energy structure of hyperelasticity and employs a hybrid quantum classical framework in which the energy functional is evaluated using parameterized quantum circuits and optimized through classical routines. To enable implementation on current quantum hardware, polynomial approximations of the nonlinear strain energy density are introduced, yielding a representation compatible with variational quantum algorithms. The methodology is demonstrated on a one dimensional NeoHookean material model using finite element discretizations with first and second order shape functions and nonhomogeneous boundary conditions. Numerical experiments investigate the influence of the polynomial approximation order on the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed approach, illustrating its feasibility for near term quantum devices.

infographic.key_insight: The paper reformulates nonlinear finite element analysis of hyperelastic materials as a hybrid variational quantum optimization problem by approximating the strain energy with polynomials that a NISQ device can evaluate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It suggests a possible path to solving nonlinear elasticity problems on near-term quantum hardware, potentially useful for computational mechanics workflows where classical solvers are costly.
method: Uses the hyperelastic potential energy functional as the objective for a variational quantum algorithm.
Represents nonlinear strain energy with polynomial approximations to make it compatible with parameterized quantum circuits.
Solves a 1D NeoHookean finite element example with first- and second-order shape functions and nonhomogeneous boundary conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments that compare polynomial approximation orders and assess accuracy and efficiency for the 1D NeoHookean benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on polynomial approximation quality, so accuracy and scalability may degrade for more complex nonlinear materials or higher-dimensional finite element problems.
infographic.paper_title: A Variational Quantum Algorithm for Nonlinear Finite Element Analysis of Hyperelastic Materials

title: Permutation Matrix Representation for Quantum Simulation: Comparative Resource Analysis
authors: Hriday Sabharwal, Itay Hen
abstract: We present a comparative study of the permutation matrix representation (PMR) method for Hamiltonian simulation alongside other leading quantum algorithms. Our analysis focuses on resource costs for simulating both time-independent and time-dependent Hamiltonians. For the time-independent case, we benchmark PMR against quantum signal processing (QSP) and qubitization, using the Rydberg interaction Hamiltonian as a representative example. For the time-dependent case, we compare the time-dependent extension of PMR with the quantum highly oscillatory protocol (qHOP), applied to a Floquet-driven transverse field Ising model in arbitrary spatial dimensions. In both regimes, we find that PMR offers complementary advantages in resource requirements and exhibits favorable scaling with certain system parameters, suggesting that it may provide practical benefits on resource-constrained quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Permutation Matrix Representation (PMR) is a competitive Hamiltonian-simulation approach that can offer complementary resource advantages versus QSP, qubitization, and qHOP, especially in resource-constrained settings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study gives quantum hardware designers a practical basis for choosing simulation algorithms by comparing gate/resource costs for both static and driven Hamiltonians.
method: Benchmarked PMR against QSP and qubitization for time-independent Hamiltonians.
Compared time-dependent PMR with qHOP on a Floquet-driven transverse field Ising model.
Used the Rydberg interaction Hamiltonian as the static reference and the driven Ising model across arbitrary spatial dimensions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The evaluation is comparative and resource-focused, with conclusions drawn from benchmark analysis of simulated Hamiltonian classes rather than experimental hardware runs.
infographic.watch_item: PMR’s advantages are problem- and parameter-dependent, so its practical benefit may vary with the Hamiltonian structure and available hardware resources.
infographic.paper_title: Permutation Matrix Representation for Quantum Simulation: Comparative Resource Analysis

title: Rademacher Complexity Bounds for Parameterized Quantum Circuits Generated by Pauli Strings
authors: Hiroshi Ohno
abstract: In this study, we analyze the Rademacher complexity $ \mathcal{R}_{M} $ of a parameterized unitary whose generators are chosen from $ n $-qubit Pauli strings. Although generalization bounds for quantum machine learning models have been studied in several settings, explicit Rademacher-complexity bounds for parameterized unitaries generated by Pauli strings remain less transparent. We derive simple scaling bounds in terms of the number of parameters $ L $ and the number of training samples $ M $: $ \mathcal{O}(\frac{L^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\sqrt{M}}) $ for the full parameter domain and $ \mathcal{O}(\frac{L}{\sqrt{M}}) $ for a restricted parameter domain. Furthermore, we compare the obtained results with those for a classical linear model class and suggest a potential statistical-complexity advantage when the norms of both the input and the parameter in the classical model scale with the number of parameters. Numerical experiments provide qualitative evidence consistent with the predicted scaling.

infographic.key_insight: The paper derives explicit Rademacher-complexity scaling bounds for parameterized quantum circuits built from Pauli-string generators, showing how generalization capacity grows with parameter count and shrinks with sample size.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These bounds give a practical complexity estimate for quantum machine-learning circuits, helping engineers anticipate when adding more trainable gates may hurt generalization.
method: Analyze the Rademacher complexity of parameterized unitaries whose generators are n-qubit Pauli strings.
Derive asymptotic bounds for two regimes: full parameter domain and restricted parameter domain.
Compare the quantum model class to a classical linear model class to assess relative statistical complexity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical derivations supported by numerical experiments that provide qualitative evidence consistent with the predicted scaling laws.
infographic.watch_item: The results are scaling bounds rather than tight finite-sample guarantees, so actual performance may depend on circuit structure, parameter constraints, and problem-specific data distributions.
infographic.paper_title: Rademacher Complexity Bounds for Parameterized Quantum Circuits Generated by Pauli Strings

title: Quantum Subliminal Learning
authors: Shi-Xin Zhang, Yu-Qin Chen
abstract: Machine learning models can inherit hidden behavioral traits through innocuous public interfaces, a phenomenon known as subliminal learning. Here we extend this framework to quantum models and study two distillation pathways: an auxiliary channel on random inputs and a restricted task channel in which the student matches a public supervised output while the hidden behavior resides on a disjoint task. Both classical and quantum neural networks (QNNs) exhibit efficient auxiliary-channel subliminal learning, but the task channel shows strong architecture dependence. Classical neural networks transmit little hidden-task information through the public-task interface, whereas QNNs retain most of the hidden-task signal. We show that a unified geometric picture explains both regimes: transmission is controlled by the teacher drift magnitude together with the fraction of hidden-task-relevant drift that remains visible through the public interface. These results identify a concrete security concern for quantum model supply chains and suggest a controlled route for hidden-information transfer in quantum information processing.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum models can unintentionally transmit hidden behavior through public outputs, with QNNs preserving much more hidden-task information than classical networks in restricted-task settings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This raises a practical security risk for quantum model supply chains, while also enabling controlled hidden-information transfer in quantum information workflows.
method: Study two subliminal-learning pathways: an auxiliary channel on random inputs and a restricted task channel on disjoint hidden vs. public tasks.
Compare classical neural networks and quantum neural networks under both channels to measure hidden behavior transfer.
Use a geometric explanation based on teacher drift magnitude and the visible fraction of hidden-task-relevant drift.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports efficient auxiliary-channel subliminal learning for both classical and quantum models, but strong architecture dependence in the task channel, with QNNs retaining most hidden-task signal while classical networks transmit little.
infographic.watch_item: The main limitation is architecture-dependent behavior: results from one QNN/classical setup may not generalize to all model designs or deployment settings.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Subliminal Learning

title: Automated Unitary Coupled Cluster Circuit Design via Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search
authors: Jianpeng Chen, Zirui Sheng, Cunxi Gong, Weitang Li
abstract: Designing compact and accurate circuits for the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) is a central challenge in near-term quantum chemistry. Existing adaptive methods such as ADAPT-VQE design circuits by iteratively selecting operators from a predefined pool guided by gradient information and greedy heuristics. In this work, we adopt differentiable quantum architecture search (DQAS) as a circuit design framework based on the UCCSD operator pool, and introduce two complementary strategies: a global mode that simultaneously optimizes all operator selections, and a layerwise mode that constructs circuits incrementally while preserving previously learned structure. By relaxing discrete operator selection into a continuous differentiable optimization, DQAS enables gradient-based exploration over the combinatorial space of UCC circuit architectures. Benchmarks on BeH2, H4, LiH, H6, and H2O (8-14 qubits) show that both strategies achieve higher accuracy and fewer CNOT gates than ADAPT-VQE in the compact circuit regime, with up to 2.7-fold accuracy improvement for H2O and CNOT reductions of 13-17% at equivalent circuit depths. Benchmarks on the qubit-excitation-based (QEB) operator pool confirm that both advantages generalize beyond UCCSD. These results demonstrate that differentiable architecture search provides an effective and generalizable framework for designing accurate and compact VQE circuits in near-term quantum chemistry.

infographic.key_insight: Differentiable quantum architecture search can automatically design compact UCC-based VQE circuits that are more accurate than greedy adaptive selection methods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical path to lower-CNOT, higher-fidelity quantum chemistry circuits for near-term hardware, improving the viability of VQE workflows.
method: Relax discrete operator choice into a continuous differentiable optimization problem.
Use a UCCSD operator pool with two search modes: global and layerwise.
Evaluate learned architectures against ADAPT-VQE and also test on a QEB operator pool.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across BeH2, H4, LiH, H6, and H2O on 8-14 qubits, the method improved accuracy and reduced CNOT count, including up to 2.7× better accuracy for H2O and 13-17% fewer CNOTs at similar depth.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on the quality of the operator pool and the optimization landscape, so scaling and convergence behavior may vary on larger or noisier hardware targets.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Unitary Coupled Cluster Circuit Design via Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search
